Pharmaceutical Sciences (Shenzhen), Sun Yat-sen University Shenzhen China ([ROR:0064kty71](https://ror.org/0064kty71)) † Corresponding author ## Abstract MCM8 and MCM9 form a functional helicase complex (MCM8/9) that plays an essential role in DNA homologous recombination repair for DNA double-strand break. However, the structural characterization of MCM8/9 for DNA binding/unwinding remains unclear. Here, we report structures of the MCM8/9 complex using cryo-electron microscopy single particle analysis. The structures reveal that MCM8/9 is arranged into a heterohexamer through a threefold symmetry axis, creating a central channel that accommodates DNA. Multiple characteristic hairpins from the N-terminal oligosaccharide/oligonucleotide (OB) domains of MCM8/9 protrude into the central channel and serve to unwind the duplex DNA. When activated by HROB, the structure of MCM8/9’s N-tier ring converts its symmetry from C3 to C1 with a conformational change that expands the MCM8/9’s trimer interface. Moreover, our structural dynamic analyses revealed that the flexible C-tier ring exhibited rotary motions relative to the N-tier ring, which is required for the unwinding ability of MCM8/9. In summary, our structural and biochemistry study provides a basis for understanding the DNA unwinding mechanism of MCM8/9 helicase in homologous recombination. ## Introduction DNA helicases play critical roles in multiple cellular processes including DNA replication, transcription, recombination, and repair. Dysfunction of multiple DNA helicases has been correlated with various human diseases including cancers, Bloom Syndrome, Werner Syndrome, Fanconi Anemia, reproductive deficiencies, and infertility, etc (Brosh and Matson, 2020; Heyer et al., 2010). One of the most extensively studied subfamilies of DNA helicases is the minichromosome maintenance (MCM) proteins. In the human genome, the MCM family contains two subgroups of AAA+ ATPase/helicase complexes, consisting of eight MCM members (MCM2-9) (Maiorano et al., 2006). Structural studies of these complexes are critical for elucidating their mechanisms. The hexameric MCM2-7 complex, also known as a replicative helicase, play a vital role in the initiation and elongation of eukaryotic chromosome replication. Previous structural and biochemical studies have revealed that the MCM2-7 complex exhibits high structural flexibility during DNA replication (Yuan and Li, 2020). It can adopt multiple conformations by interacting with its loaders and activators to form different intermediates, including the helicase-loading intermediate Orc-Cdc6-Cdt1-MCM2-7 (OCCM), the inactive MCM2-7 Double Hexamer (DH) and the active replicative helicase complex Cdc45-MCM2-7-GINS (CMG) (Yuan et al., 2017; Miller et al., 2019; Li et al., 2015; Abid Ali et al., 2016). For loading onto DNA, the apo MCM2-7 hexamer first binds to the licensing factor Cdt1. In the presence of ATP, the initiators ORC and Cdc6 assemble on the origin DNA to form an active loading platform and load the Cdt1-bound MCM2-7 onto DNA to form the OCCM complex (Yuan and Li, 2020). The origin DNA is encircled into the central channel of the MCM2-7 hexamer via the MCM2-MCM5 entry ‘gate’ (Samel et al., 2014). While ATP hydrolysis occurs in OCCM, it seems that Cdt1, Cdc6, and ORC are released in sequential disassembly steps, and then the first loaded MCM2-7 encircling DNA recruits a second ORC-Cdc6 complex, which in turn loads the second Cdt1-bound MCM2-7 to form a head-to-head MCM2-7 DH (Yuan and Li, 2020). During double-hexamer assembly, the N-tier ring of MCM2-7 rotates by nearly 30° when aligned with the MCM2-7 hexamer in its loading intermediate OCCM (Noguchi et al., 2017). As the MCM2-7 double hexamer on DNA is inactive, lots of regulators along with the helicase activators Cdc45 and GINS complex, are required to convert the double hexamer into two activated CMG replicative helicases that translocate along the leading strands with a bi-directional replication mechanism (Georgescu et al., 2017; Eickhoff et al., 2019; Douglas et al., 2018). The aforementioned structural studies have also revealed that layers of characteristic hairpin loops inside the chamber of MCM2-7 hexamer, including the helix-2 insertion loops (H2I), the presensor-1 (PS1) as well as β-turn motifs of oligosaccharide/oligonucleotide (OB) domains, contribute to DNA binding and separation (Slaymaker and Chen, 2012). Additionally, another allosteric communication loop (ACL) conserved in all MCM helicases was also found to be important for helicase activity. The ACL mediates inter-subunit interactions between the N-terminal DNA processing domain and the C-terminal AAA+ motor domain (Sakakibara et al., 2008; Barry et al., 2009). MCM8 and MCM9 make up the other helicase complex, which is the homolog of MCM2-7 (Nishimura et al., 2012). In contrast to the replicative helicase MCM2-7, MCM8 and MCM9 function as a DNA helicase complex (MCM8/9) in HR-mediated DNA repair for DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) and DNA interstrand crosslinks (ICLs) (Lutzmann et al., 2012). Several studies have suggested that cells lacking MCM8 and MCM9 are highly sensitive to DNA cross-linking reagents (Morii et al., 2019; McKinzey et al., 2021). The MCM8 and MCM9 knock-out mice were found to be sterile and revealed gametogenesis deficiency as well as chromosomal damage due to impaired HR (Lutzmann et al., 2012). During HR repair, MCM8/9 was rapidly recruited to the DNA damage sites and colocalized with the recombinase Rad51 (Park et al., 2013). It also interacted with the nuclease complex MRN (MRE11-RAD50-NBS1), which was required for DNA resection at DSBs to facilitate HR repair (Lee et al., 2015). Recently, HROB (also known as C17orf53 or MCM8IP) has been identified as an essential factor in loading the MCM8/9 complex to the sites of DNA damage and stimulating its helicase activity to promote replication fork progression during DNA recombination and replication. Loss of HROB led to HR defects because it is necessary for the recruitment and activation of MCM8/9 (Hustedt et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2020). The HROB harbors a flexible N-terminal domain (NTD), a central proline-rich region (PRR) and an OB-fold domain at the C-terminus. It was reported that the MCM8/9 binding motif (MBM) is embedded in the PRR region and binds to the NTD domains of MCM8/9 (Huang et al., 2020). Although progress has been made in understanding the role of MCM8/9 HR during the past decade, the structure-function relationship, especially the structural characterization of MCM8/9 helicase activity, remains unknown. Notably, MCM8/9 is composed of two subunits, MCM8 and MCM9. It is challenging to extrapolate its role through a simple comparison with MCM2-7, which consists of six subunits. MCM8 and MCM9 proteins are structurally similar, with an MCM domain at the N-terminus (NTD) and an AAA+ ATPase domain at the C-terminus (CTD). The NTD and CTD are connected by flexible linkers (N-C linkers), which allow the movement of the AAA+ domain during unwinding (Brewster et al., 2008). The NTDs of MCM8 and MCM9 share an analogous domain organization and can be divided into three domains: the zinc finger domain (ZF), the helical domain (HD), and the OB domain. In addition to the AAA+ ATPase domain, MCM8 possesses an additional WHD domain in the CTD while MCM9 contains a putative helix-turn-helix (HTH) domain and an extensional C-tail at the C-terminus (Griffin and Trakselis, 2019). In the previous study, we reported a 6.6 Å cryo-EM structure of the human MCM8/9 (hMCM8/9) NTD ring. We also analyzed the crystal structures of MCM8 and MCM9 NTDs separately, which exhibited conformational changes when assembled into the MCM8/9 hexamer (Li et al., 2021). However, the low-resolution structure of the MCM8/9 NTD ring is insufficient to fully illustrate the assembly and activation mechanisms of the MCM8/9 hexamer. Here, we present a near-atomic resolution structure of the chicken MCM8/9 (gMCM8/9) complex and a 3.95 Å cryo-EM structure of the human MCM8/9 NTD ring under HROB induction. Based on these structures, we conducted further investigation on the structural features of the DNA-binding region of MCM8/9 and the conformational changes required for its activation by HROB. Our structural and biochemical studies shed light on the structural and functional relationship of the MCM8/9 helicase. ## Results ### Overall structure of the gMCM8/9 helicase complex As our previous study shows the hMCM8/9 helicase complex is unstable for high-resolution structure determination, we first solved the cryo-EM structure of the MCM8/9 complex from Gallus gallus. The structure reveals that gMCM8 and gMCM9 alternately assemble into a pinwheel-like hexamer with a central channel. The trimerization of the gMCM8/9 heterodimer is in line with our previously reported hMCM8/9 structure at 6.6 Å resolution (Li et al., 2021). When we performed structural superposition, the NTD ring of gMCM8/9 superimposes well onto that of hMCM8/9, indicating that eukaryotic MCM8 and MCM9 form a conserved hexamer complex during evolution (Figure 1—figure supplements 2–4). The diameter of the NTD ring is ~132 Å and that of the inner channel is ~28 Å which is large enough to accommodate dsDNA to pass through (Figure 1C and S5). The assembly pattern of the gMCM8/9 complex with a threefold (C3) symmetry axis is unique among MCM helicases. It arranges the three MCM8 and three MCM9 in the same planes, enclosing a channel with multiple symmetrical hairpins. This assembly pattern differs from that of the eukaryotic MCM2-7 heterohexamer with non-symmetry and the archaeal MCM homohexamer with sixfold symmetry (Li et al., 2015; Fletcher et al., 2003). In addition, a distinguishing feature of the gMCM8/9 is that the helical domain of gMCM8 contains a long α5 helix that protrudes around the hexameric ring (Figure 1B). The domain structures of gMCM8/9’s, including the MCM domains, the AAA+ motor domains, and the WH domain, fit well into their electron density maps (Figure 1—figure supplement 5). For each gMCM8/9 heterodimer, the positions of characteristic hairpin loops of MCM helicase, such as H2I, PS1, OB hairpins (referred to as OB-hps), and the ACL were well defined. Among them, the OB-hps extend to the central channel, while the ACLs are close to the H2I and PS1 hairpins within the AAA+ domains (Figure 1B). ### The assembly of gMCM8 and gMCM9 in the NTD ring As our structural analysis revealed that the gMCM8/9 hexamer is the trimerization of the MCM8/9 heterodimer, this leads to the formation of three dimer interfaces within each MCM8/9 heterodimer and three putative trimer interfaces between each neighboring MCM8/9 heterodimer (Figure 2A). The high-resolution structure of the gMCM8/9 NTD ring allows us to analyze these two types of interfaces in detail, which serve as the structural basis of MCM8/9 assembly. ![Figure 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/87468/elife-87468-fig2-v1.jpg) **Figure 2.:** (A) The cutoff structure of the gMCM8/9 NTD presents in the cartoon. The dimer interface and trimer interface were indicated by boxes with dotted lines and solid lines, respectively. (B, C) The dimer interface (B) and trimer interface (C) were mediated by hydrophobic interaction and polar interactions. The interaction details between gMCM8 and gMCM9 in two interfaces are shown in stereo view. ![Figure 2—figure supplement 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/87468/elife-87468-fig2-figsupp1-v1.jpg) **Figure 2—figure supplement 1.:** (A and B) The region-mediated hydrophobic interaction in Figure 2B. (A) (MCM8), (B) (MCM9). (C and D) The region-mediated hydrophobic interaction in Figure 2C. (C) (MCM8), (D) (MCM9). The key residues were in bold. The dimer interface between NTDs of gMCM8 and gMCM9 is largely composed of the β-strands from the OB domain of gMCM9 and the flanking ZF and OB domain of gMCM8. Both the polar and hydrophobic interactions between respective β-strands are responsible for the binding of the MCM8/9 dimer. For example, the side chains of R220gMCM9 and Q248gMCM9 form hydrogen bonds with the carbonyl groups in the main chains of I172gMCM8 and T226gMCM8, respectively. In addition, the main chain of T119gMCM9 also forms a hydrogen bond with the neighboring carbonyl group in the side chain of D228gMCM8. Furthermore, the benzene ring of F253gMCM9 inserts into a hydrophobic pocket surrounded by residues L179, P217, F181, L201, and Y199 from gMCM8 and W250 from gMCM9, which further stabilize the interaction between gMCM8 and gMCM9 (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B). Compared to the strong interaction between the dimer interface, the interaction within the trimer interface is weaker. The trimer interface is dominated by electrostatic interaction and hydrogen-bonding interactions. The side chain of R152gMCM8 forms salt bridges with both the side chains of D200gMCM9 and D232gMCM9. In addition, the side chain of K158gMCM8 forms a hydrogen bond with the side chain of E37gMCM9 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D). Based on the preceding analysis, we assume that opening a ‘gate’ on the trimer interface for DNA loading will be easier than on the dimer interface. Taken together, these interactions facilitate and stabilize the assembly of the NTD hexameric ring of gMCM8/9. ### Structural comparison of MCM8/9 and MCM2-7 To explore the functional state of gMCM8/9, we performed structural comparisons between gMCM8/9 and various MCM2-7-containing complexes. We first compared the gMCM8/9 structure with MCM2-7 in the OCCM complex by aligning their respective C-tier rings. As shown in Figure 3A, the NTDs of gMCM8/9 fit well with those of MCM7, MCM3, and MCM5, but rotated slightly in the following MCM2, MCM6 and MCM4. This minor variation is due to the opening ‘gate’ of the MCM5-MCM2 interface in the OCCM complex. When superimposing the hexameric gMCM8/9 complex onto one hexamer of the MCM2-7 DH, we found that the two C-tier rings aligned well while their N-tier rings had a ~30° clockwise rotation (Figure 3B and C). Such rotation could be caused by the two hexameric complex’s different assembly patterns. A more plausible explanation is that the assembly of the MCM2-7 DH induces the conformational change in its N-tier ring (Noguchi et al., 2017). We also compared the gMCM8/9 structure with that of MCM2-7 in the apo CMG complex and found that the NTD ring has a similar translation and rotation but slighter than in comparison with MCM2-7 DH (data not shown). As the NTD ring of MCM2-7 that transits from the DH to the CMG just requires a small domain translation (Yuan et al., 2016). Overall, our structure of gMCM8/9 was conformationally similar to the structure of the MCM2-7 complex in its loading intermediate OCCM rather than that in the DH. This is also consistent with previous findings that the recombinant MCM8/9 complex alone exhibited limited helicase activity in vitro (Huang et al., 2020). Therefore, we presume the current structure of gMCM8/9 may represent a loading state of MCM8/9 helicase. ![Figure 3.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/87468/elife-87468-fig3-v1.jpg) **Figure 3.:** (A) The gMCM8/9 hexamer (green cyan and slate) was aligned to the MCM2-7 hexamer (light pink) from the Orc-Cdc6-Cdt1-MCM2-7 (OCCM) complex. The N-tier rings comparison are presented here with a slight rotation beginning at MCM5-MCM2 ’Gate’ and the following MCM6 and MCM4. The ‘Gate’ was indicated by the black arrow. (B, C) Structural superposition of the gMCM8/9 hexamer to the MCM2-7 double hexamer (wheat) by aligning their respective C-tier ring. The bottom view (B) and top view (C) are shown respectively. Note the ~30° clockwise rotation of the gMCM8/9 N-tier ring compared to that of MCM2-7. ### HROB activates MCM8/9 probably by inducing a conformational change of its NTD ring To explore the activation mechanism of hMCM8/9, we examined its activity in the presence of OB-fold containing protein HROB (Figure 4A). Using a helicase assay, we found that the HROB-MBM motif was unable to stimulate the helicase activity of hMCM8/9. However, its CTD, which includes the OB-fold domain, could significantly activate hMCM8/9 (Figure 4B). The HROB-CTD not only directly interacts with hMCM8/9 NTD, but also forms a complex with it, as confirmed by the GST pulldown assay (Figure 4C). ![Figure 4.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/87468/elife-87468-fig4-v1.jpg) **Figure 4.:** (A) Domain organization of human HROB. (B) Local resolution distributions of hMCM8/9 NTD. ![Figure 4—figure supplement 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/87468/elife-87468-fig4-figsupp2-v1.jpg) We collected the complex formed by the HROB-CTD and hMCM8/9 NTD proteins described above and reconstructed their structure using cryo-electron microscopy (Figure 4D, Table 2, Materials and methods). Unfortunately, the density map of HROB-CTD was not observed in the reconstruction. And the 3.95 Å structure of the hMCM8/9 NTD ring was reconstructed with C1 symmetry, in contrast to the structure of gMCM8/9, which has C3 symmetry (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). We also found that the structure of the hMCM8/9 NTD ring underwent a large conformational change when compared to the previously described hMCM8/9 NTD (Li et al., 2021). As a result, the two conformations were designated as Conformation I (hMCM8/9 NTD at 6.6 Å) and Conformation II (hMCM8/9 NTD at 3.95 Å) (Figure 4E and F). In line with our observation, when superimposed these two conformations of hMCM8/9 NTD, we found that one of the trimer interfaces in Conformation II was expanded by ~5 Å (Figure 4G). This expansion further pushed its neighboring MCM8/9 heterodimers to shift to either side. The left dimer translates downward by ~8 Å and tilts by ~6° while the right one shifts by ~7 Å and tilts by ~8° (Figure 4I and J). Interestingly, the ZF of MCM8 shifts by ~3 Å to the left, and the ZF of MCM9 shifts by ~4.5 Å to the right, resulting in an overall expansion of ~6 Å (Figure 4G). Notably, the N-tier ring of MCM2-7 from the CMG-DNA complex translates laterally by ~12 Å and tilts by ~12° when compared to the structure of MCM2-7 DH (Noguchi et al., 2017). Without DNA, the C-tier ring of MCM2-7 from the apo CMG also adopts two different conformations including tilted and untilted, indicating a conformational change of MCM2-7 during activation (Yuan et al., 2016). Based on the above observations and the stimulation effect of HROB on the helicase activity of MCM8/9, we propose that HROB activates MCM8/9 by inducing a conformational change of its NTD ring. ### Spatial distribution and functional role of the OB-fold hairpins As the hairpin loops of OB-fold domains are essential for DNA binding and/or unwinding in the reported hexameric MCM helicase complexes (Slaymaker and Chen, 2012), we analyzed the two types of hairpin loops from OB domains in the NTD rings of gMCM8/9 and hMCM8/9. The first type of OB hairpins of gMCM8 and gMCM9 (refer to OB-hp) protrude into the central chamber in a threefold symmetry manner and narrow down the channel (Figure 5A). In particular, the OB-hp of gMCM8/9 forms two layers. The three OB-hp of gMCM8 form the upper layer and the three gMCM9 OB-hp comprise the lower layer (Figure 5C). We found that MCM8 and MCM9 form a single heterohexameric ring with a centric channel that allows the DNA to pass through. The OB hairpin loops within the centric channel may be involved in interacting with and separating substrate DNA. The N-C linkers of MCM8/9 play important roles in helicase activity. Notably, the regulator HROB induces a conformational change of the MCM8/9 NTD ring, which may underlie the helicase activation. MCM8/9 and MCM2-7 are both MCM proteins with highly conserved domain organization and sequence similarity (Maiorano et al., 2006; Maiorano et al., 2005). Compared with the heterohexameric structure of MCM2-7, the MCM8/9 hexamer is arranged in an alternate mode with the threefold symmetry axis. Interestingly, it was reported that the Escherichia coli helicase DnaB also exists in a quaternary state with C3 or C6 symmetry and can change the symmetry states reversibly depending on the pH value of the buffers or the presence of nucleotides (Donate et al., 2000). It has been proposed that the symmetry transition plays a role in the loading of regulators on DNA and is directly linked to DNA translocation (Yang et al., 2002; Núñez-Ramírez et al., 2006). Similarly, we doubt that MCM8/9 changes its symmetry from C3 to C1 symmetry in the presence of HROB. In other words, helicases may orchestrate the inner channels by controlling the relative positions of subunits, assisting in DNA loading and unwinding. Taking inspiration from the structural and unwinding mechanisms of MCM2-7, we also investigated the key elements of MCM8/9 involved in DNA interaction or separation. In the central channel of the MCM2-7 complex, several structural elements involved in DNA binding and strand separation were illustrated by a series of CMG structures complexed with different types of DNA (Yuan and Li, 2020). According to recent research, the OB hairpin loops of MCM3, MCM4, MCM6, and MCM7 form ‘dam-and-diversion tunnel’ to block and divert the lagging strand from the leading strand (Yuan and Li, 2020). For the MCM8/9 complex, the OB-hps of MCM8 and MCM9 are essential for DNA unwinding. They form a two-layered structure with threefold symmetry. In which, three OB-hps of MCM9 form the upper layer, while three OB-hps of MCM8 form the lower layer, suggesting a synergistic mechanism for MCM8/9 OB hairpins to interact with DNA. When modeled a forked DNA into the channel, the OB-hp loops make very close contact with the DNA strand that passes through the channel, capable of inserting their loops into the major or minor grooves of the DNA in a sequential manner. While in the Conformation II of hMCM8/9 NTD ring, the OB-hps of hMCM8 and hMCM9 lose their C3 symmetry without significant conformational change. This symmetry transition could be caused by HROB while inducing trimer interface expansion. In addition, the highly conserved residue F363 from the OB hairpin loop of MCM7 serves as a strand separation pin to unwind forked DNA via making a π-π interaction with DNA (Baretić et al., 2020). The highly conserved phenylalanine was also found on the OB-hps of MCM8 and MCM9 (F353 of hMCM8, F251 of hMCM9) (Figure 5D). They will most likely perform functions similar to those found in MCM2-7. We also present a new conformation (Conformation II) of the MCM8/9 NTD ring induced by HROB, which may enhance the DNA binding ability of the MCM8/9 complex. We found that when MCM8/9 is complexed with the CTD domain of HROB, it becomes more stable and exhibits significantly higher helicase activity. The HROB CTD domain is about 20 kDa and is composed of a flexible loop and an OB-fold domain. The flexible loop containing ~20 amino acids is sufficient to interact with the MCM8/9 complex, but it alone is unable to stimulate the helicase activity of MCM8/9 (Huang et al., 2020). Our helicase assay demonstrated that the OB-fold domain of HROB is required for MCM8/9 activation. The OB-fold domain is a nucleic acid-binding motif that likely help to load the DNA into the central channel of MCM8/9. Induced by HROB, the structure of the MCM8/9 NTD ring convert its C3 symmetry to C1, and two of the MCM8/9 heterodimers translate and tilt following the expansion of the trimer interface. When the MCM2-7 double hexamer encircles the double-stranded origin DNA, the MCM5-MCM2 interface characterizes as a ‘gate’ that undergoes open and closed conformation change to engage the DNA entry (Samel et al., 2014). The expansion of the MCM8/9 trimer interface may involve a transient conformation state to facilitate the DNA entry into the inner channel of the MCM8/9 hexamer. Thus, HROB not only aids in the loading of DNA into MCM8/9, but also acts as an activator, collaborating with MCM8/9 to promote DNA unwinding. Benefiting from the rapid development of cryo-electron microscopy technology over the past decade, a dozen structures of MCM2-7-containing intermediates have been resolved including the OCCM, DH, and CMG with/ without DNA (Yuan and Li, 2020). Based on these structures, the hand-over-hand rotary mode and the ‘dam-and-diversion tunnel’ model had been proposed for MCM2-7 helicase in DNA translocation and unwinding (Yuan and Li, 2020; Eickhoff et al., 2019). For MCM8/9 helicase, there is currently no established model to describe its unwinding mechanism. Here, our structural and biochemical studies have provided some hints in this regard. First of all, the structural dynamics analysis reveals that the MCM8/9 CTD ring rotates relative to the NTD ring. Second, the length of the MCM8 and MCM9 N-C linkers are surprisingly much longer than those of the MCM2-7 complex, which may permit the rotations of MCM8/9. The fact that single-site structure-guided mutations on the ACL loops have no effect on the helicase activity of MCM8/9 further supports the idea that the N-C linkers, rather than the ACL loop, mediated the interaction between the N-tier ring and the C-tier ring of MCM8/9. Last but not least, HROB can convert inactive MCM8/9 into an active helicase by recruiting and inducing a conformational change in the MCM8/9 NTD ring. Although a rotary model is in sight and our findings also hint at a distinct unwinding mechanism of MCM8/9, many questions remain unsolved. The most pressing issue is that the type of DNA substrate unwound by MCM8/9 is unknown. In vivo sequencing and in vitro DNA binding results are required to screen appropriate substrates. Furthermore, as the HROB only stimulates ~60% of the MCM8/9 helicase in vitro, we believe that other regulators remain to be discover for the full activation of MCM8/9 helicase. Based on these results, the high-resolution structures of MCM8/9 with DNA in the presence of ADP or ATP are necessary to fully clarify the unwinding mechanism of MCM8/9. Despite these limitations, the MCM8/9 complex structures provided in this study will be a rich source of information for further research into the mechanism of DNA helicase in homologous recombination, as well as for the analysis of multiple disease mutations in MCM8/9 associated with premature ovarian failure as well as cancers. ## Materials and methods ### Plasmids The human MCM8/9 genes were obtained by reverse transcription of mRNA from HeLa cells. ## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.87468.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.87468.3.sa1)

MCM8 and MCM9 are paralogues of the eukaryotic MCM2-7 proteins. MCM2-7 form a heterohexameric complex to function as a replicative helicase while MCM8-9 form another hexameric helicase complex that may function in homologous recombination-mediated long-tract gene conversion and/or break-induced replication. MCM2-7 complex is loaded during the low Cdk period by ORC, CDC6, and Cdt1, when the origin DNA may intrude into the central channel via the MCM2-MCM5 entry "gate". In the S phase, MCM2-7 complex is activated as CMG helicase with the help of CDC45 and GINS complex. On the other hand, it still remains unclear how MCM8-9 complex is loaded onto DNA and then activated.

In this study, the authors first investigated the cryo-EM structure of chicken MCM8-9 (gMCM8-9) complex. Based on the data obtained, they suggest that the observed gMCM8-9 structure might represent the structure of a loading state with possible DNA entry "gate". The authors further investigated the cryo-EM structure of human MCM8-9 (hMCM8-9) complex in the presence of the activator protein, HROB, and compared the structure with that obtained without HROB1, which the authors published previously. As a result, they suggest that MCM8-9 complex may change the conformation upon HROB binding, leading to helicase activation. Furthermore, based on the structural analyses, they identified some important residues and motifs in MCM8-9 complex, mutations of which actually impaired the MCM8-9 activity in vitro and in vivo.

Overall, the data presented would support the authors' conclusions and would be of wide interest for those working in the fields of DNA replication and repair. One caveat is that most of the structural data are shown only as ribbon model without showing the density map data obtained by cryo-EM, which makes accurate evaluation of the data somewhat difficult.

Addition after review of the revised manuscript: The authors have made a reasonable attempt to address the points raised by the reviewers, by which the paper is significantly improved.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.87468.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.87468.3.sa2)

MCM8 and MCM9 together form a hexameric DNA helicase that is involved in homologous recombination (HR) for repairing DNA double-strand breaks. The authors have previously reported on the winged-helix structure of the MCM8 (Zeng et al. BBRC, 2020) and the N-terminal structure of MCM8/9 hexametric complex (MCM8/9-NTD) (Li et al. Structure, 2021). This manuscript reports the structure of a near-complete MCM8/9 complex and the conformational change of MCM8/9-NTD in the presence of its binding protein, HROB, as well as the residues important for its helicase activity.

The presented data might potentially explain how MCM8/9 works as a helicase. However, additional studies are required to conclude this point because the presented MCM8/9 structure is not a DNA-bound form and HROB is not visible in the presented structural data. Taking into these accounts, this work will be of interest to biologists studying DNA transactions.

A strength of this paper is that the authors revealed the near-complete MCM8/9 structure with 3.66A and 5.21A for the NTD and CTD, respectively (Figure 1). Additionally, the authors discovered a conformational change in the MCM8/9-NTD when HROB was included (Figure 4) and a flexible nature of MCM8/9-CTD (Figure S6 and Movie 1).

The revised version of "Structural and mechanistic insights into the MCM8/9 helicase complex" by Weng et al. includes only very minor changes in the text and incorporates two additional supplementary figures (S8 and S11) illustrating the size of MCM8/9 mutants.

In the previous version, I raised two important concerns that required addressing. (1) The presented structures exclusively depicted the unbound forms of DNA. It is crucial to elucidate the structure of a DNA-bound form. (2) The MCM8/9 activator, HROB, was not visible in the structural data. Although HROB induced a conformational change in MCM8/9-NTD, it is essential to visualize the structure of an MCM8/9-HROB complex.

The authors neither addressed nor provided new data in response to these issues. Consequently, I maintain my initial stance and have no further comments on the revised version.

results.result: The gMCM8/9 complex forms a heterohexamer with C3 symmetry, consisting of alternating MCM8 and MCM9 subunits arranged around a central channel (~28 Å diameter) capable of accommodating dsDNA. This structure was determined at 3.66 Å (NTD) and 5.21 Å (CTD) resolution using cryo-EM.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C30-C36 are well-supported by cryo-EM structural data at near-atomic resolution (C31). The C3 symmetry arrangement (C2, C33) is directly observed in the density maps, and the channel dimensions (C32) are measured from the structure. The unique assembly pattern compared to MCM2-7 (C33-C34) is validated through structural superposition (C34).

results.result: The gMCM8/9 hexamer contains two types of interfaces: strong dimer interfaces between MCM8 and MCM9 within each heterodimer (mediated by polar and hydrophobic interactions), and weaker trimer interfaces between neighboring heterodimers (dominated by electrostatic interactions). The weaker trimer interface is proposed as the likely DNA entry gate.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C45 provide detailed structural analysis of specific residue interactions at both interfaces, supported by the 3.66 Å resolution structure. The inference that the weaker trimer interface serves as a DNA entry gate (C46) is reasonable based on the structural analysis showing weaker interactions (C42-C43), though this remains a hypothesis requiring experimental validation.

results.result: Structural comparison reveals that gMCM8/9 resembles the MCM2-7 loading intermediate (OCCM) rather than the double hexamer (DH), with the N-tier rings showing a ~30° rotation difference when compared to MCM2-7 DH. This suggests gMCM8/9 represents a loading state, consistent with its limited helicase activity in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 are supported by structural superposition analysis (C47, C49) and comparison with published MCM2-7 structures. The interpretation that gMCM8/9 represents a loading state (C53) is reasonably inferred from the structural similarity to OCCM and the cited observation of limited helicase activity (C52), though this remains a working hypothesis.

results.result: HROB-CTD, but not HROB-MBM alone, significantly activates hMCM8/9 helicase activity and induces a conformational change in the MCM8/9 NTD ring from C3 to C1 symmetry. This involves expansion of one trimer interface by ~5 Å and repositioning of neighboring heterodimers.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C62 are supported by experimental helicase assays (C54-C55), GST pulldown data (C56), and a 3.95 Å cryo-EM structure showing C1 symmetry (C57). The detailed structural measurements of interface expansion and dimer movements (C59-C62) are based on direct structural comparison. The mechanistic interpretation linking conformational change to activation (C63) is a reasonable inference from the combined structural and biochemical data.

results.result: The OB hairpins (OB-hps) of MCM8/9 form a two-layered structure within the central channel, with positively charged residues at the tips of MCM8 OB-hps and polar residues on MCM9 OB-hps. These hairpins are essential for DNA unwinding, as demonstrated by mutagenesis studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 describe structural features directly observed in the cryo-EM structure. The functional importance (C77, C103) is supported by helicase assays showing decreased activity in OB-hp mutants (C73-C74). However, the DNA docking model (C67) is based on computational modeling rather than direct observation, introducing some uncertainty about the precise DNA-binding mode.

results.result: The allosteric communication loops (ACLs) of MCM8/9 show high conservation with archaeal MCM helicases, but mutagenesis of conserved ACL residues (E295R in hMCM8) does not affect helicase activity, suggesting that N-C linkers rather than ACLs mediate NTD-CTD interactions in MCM8/9.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 are supported by structural superposition and sequence alignment showing ACL conservation. The functional interpretation (C71, C76, C121) is based on negative mutagenesis data (C75) showing no effect of ACL mutations on helicase activity. This is a reasonable inference, though the negative result could also reflect functional redundancy or compensatory mechanisms not tested.

results.result: Multi-body refinement analysis of cryo-EM data reveals that the MCM8/9 CTD ring exhibits rotary motions relative to the NTD ring, which is proposed to be required for DNA unwinding.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81 and C119 are supported by multi-body refinement analysis of the cryo-EM dataset, a standard method for analyzing conformational heterogeneity. The lower resolution of the CTD (5.21 Å, C80) is consistent with flexibility. However, the functional interpretation that this motion is required for unwinding (C5) is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: The N-C linkers of MCM8/9 (30-40 residues) are longer than those in MCM2-7, and deletion of these linkers significantly reduces helicase activity both in vitro and in cellular resistance assays, independent of HROB presence.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C86 are supported by sequence analysis (C82) and experimental data from helicase assays (C84-C85) showing reduced activity in deletion mutants. The interpretation that longer linkers permit rotary motion (C120) is a reasonable inference connecting structural features to the observed dynamics (C81), though this remains mechanistically speculative.

results.result: MCM8/9 N-C linkers are required for cellular resistance to cisplatin-induced DNA damage. MCM8 or MCM9 knockout DT40 cells show cisplatin sensitivity that is rescued by wild-type but not N-C linker deletion mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C91 are supported by cell viability assays showing cisplatin sensitivity in knockout cells (C88), rescue by wild-type proteins (C89), and failure of N-C linker mutants to rescue (C90). The experimental design includes appropriate controls and the conclusion (C91) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: HROB activates MCM8/9 through its OB-fold domain, which is required for helicase stimulation and likely facilitates DNA loading into the MCM8/9 central channel by inducing trimer interface expansion.
results.evaluation: Claims C110, C113 are supported by helicase assay data showing that HROB-CTD (containing the OB-fold) but not HROB-MBM alone activates MCM8/9 (C54-C55). The mechanistic interpretation about DNA loading (C114-C116) is inferred from the known function of OB-fold domains and the observed conformational changes (C59-C62), representing a reasonable but not directly demonstrated hypothesis.

results.result: MCM8/9 functions as a helicase complex in homologous recombination repair of DNA double-strand breaks and interstrand crosslinks, interacting with HR factors including Rad51 and MRN complex, and requiring HROB for recruitment and activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C16-C23 summarize established knowledge about MCM8/9 function, supported by multiple citations to previous literature. These provide essential background context for the structural studies but represent prior work rather than new findings from this manuscript.

results.result: Background information on MCM helicases, including their role in diseases, the MCM2-7 replicative helicase structure and function, and the domain organization of MCM8/9 proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C15 and C24-C27 provide background information supported by citations to established literature. These are accurately presented but represent prior knowledge rather than new findings from this study.

results.result: Previous work by the authors reported a 6.6 Å cryo-EM structure of hMCM8/9 NTD and crystal structures of individual MCM8 and MCM9 NTDs showing conformational changes upon hexamer assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C29 accurately reference the authors' previous work, providing context for the current higher-resolution structures. This is appropriately cited prior work.

results.result: MCM8/9 exhibits a unique C3 symmetry arrangement compared to MCM2-7, similar to symmetry transitions observed in E. coli DnaB helicase. The authors propose that MCM8/9 changes from C3 to C1 symmetry in the presence of HROB, potentially facilitating DNA loading.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C97 comparing MCM8/9 to MCM2-7 are supported by structural data. However, the analogy to DnaB (C98-C99) is based on cited literature, and the proposed symmetry transition mechanism (C100-C101) is speculative. While C100 is supported by observing different symmetries in different conditions, the functional interpretation (C101) lacks direct experimental validation.

results.result: The OB hairpins of MCM8/9 form a two-layered structure that may interact with DNA in a synergistic manner, with conserved phenylalanine residues potentially serving as strand separation pins similar to MCM2-7.
results.evaluation: Claims C102, C108 about MCM2-7 are supported by citations. The structural observations about MCM8/9 OB-hp arrangement (C104, C106) are data-supported. However, the DNA interaction model (C105) is based on computational docking, and the proposed function of conserved phenylalanines (C109) is inferred by analogy rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: By analogy to MCM2-7, the CTD AAA+ domain of MCM8/9 is proposed to be mobile and serve as a motor domain for DNA unwinding.
results.evaluation: Claim C78 about MCM2-7 is supported by citation. The proposal that MCM8/9 CTD functions similarly (C79) is inferred from the observed rotary motion (C81) and analogy to MCM2-7, but lacks direct functional validation. This is a reasonable hypothesis but remains speculative.

results.result: Multiple structures of MCM2-7 complexes have been resolved, leading to proposed hand-over-hand rotary and dam-and-diversion tunnel models for DNA unwinding.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C118 accurately summarize prior work on MCM2-7 structures and mechanisms, supported by appropriate citations. This provides context for comparison with MCM8/9.

results.result: The authors acknowledge limitations including unknown DNA substrate specificity, incomplete activation by HROB (~60%), and the need for additional structures with DNA and nucleotides to fully understand the MCM8/9 unwinding mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C128 represent honest acknowledgment of study limitations and future research needs. The observation that HROB stimulates only ~60% of helicase activity (C125) is supported by the experimental data (C73), and the identified gaps are reasonable assessments of what remains unknown.

results.result: Wild-type hMCM8/9 shows limited helicase activity without HROB but exhibits ~6-fold stimulation with HROB, while OB-hp mutants show decreased activity even with HROB present.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C74 are directly supported by helicase assay data presented in the manuscript. The quantitative measurements and comparisons between wild-type and mutants provide clear experimental evidence for these conclusions.

results.result: Summary of main findings: MCM8/9 forms a heterohexameric ring with a central channel, OB hairpins may interact with DNA, N-C linkers are important for helicase activity, and HROB induces conformational changes that activate the helicase.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C95 accurately summarize the major findings of the study, which are supported by the combined structural, biochemical, and cellular data presented throughout the manuscript.

results.result: The authors present cryo-EM structures of chicken MCM8/9 (gMCM8/9) showing a heterohexameric arrangement with threefold (C3) symmetry, forming a central channel (~28 Å diameter) that can accommodate DNA. The NTD and CTD were reconstructed at 3.66 Å and 5.21 Å resolution, respectively. The hexamer is organized as a trimerization of MCM8/9 heterodimers, which is unique among MCM helicases.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes that 'the data presented would support the authors' conclusions' but raises a critical caveat that 'most of the structural data are shown only as ribbon model without showing the density map data obtained by cryo-EM, which makes accurate evaluation of the data somewhat difficult.' Reviewer 3 emphasizes that 'the presented MCM8/9 structure is not a DNA-bound form,' which limits the conclusions about DNA accommodation and helicase mechanism.

results.result: The authors identify OB hairpins (OB-hps) from MCM8 and MCM9 NTDs that protrude into the central channel in two layers, with positively charged residues at their tips. Molecular modeling suggests these hairpins can contact DNA and insert into grooves. Mutational analysis shows that deletion or mutation of OB-hp tip residues decreases helicase activity (~sixfold stimulation with HROB for WT, reduced for mutants), supporting their role in DNA unwinding.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states that 'the data presented would support the authors' conclusions' and notes that the authors 'identified some important residues and motifs in MCM8-9 complex, mutations of which actually impaired the MCM8-9 activity in vitro and in vivo.' The biochemical validation through helicase assays with mutants strengthens the structural inferences about OB-hp function.

results.result: The authors show that HROB-CTD (containing an OB-fold domain) activates MCM8/9 helicase activity and induces a conformational change in the MCM8/9 NTD ring. The structure of hMCM8/9 NTD with HROB-CTD (3.95 Å resolution) shows C1 symmetry instead of C3, with one trimer interface expanded by ~5 Å, causing neighboring dimers to shift and tilt. This conformational change is proposed to underlie helicase activation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 acknowledges that 'they suggest that MCM8-9 complex may change the conformation upon HROB binding, leading to helicase activation' and that the data support this conclusion. However, Reviewer 3 raises a critical concern: 'The MCM8/9 activator, HROB, was not visible in the structural data. Although HROB induced a conformational change in MCM8/9-NTD, it is essential to visualize the structure of an MCM8/9-HROB complex.' The absence of direct visualization of HROB in the structure limits the certainty of the mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: Multi-body refinement analysis reveals that the MCM8/9 CTD ring exhibits rotary motions relative to the NTD ring. The N-C linkers connecting NTD and CTD (30-40 residues) are longer than in MCM2-7. Deletion of N-C linkers significantly reduces helicase activity in vitro (with or without HROB) and impairs cellular resistance to cisplatin in vivo, indicating these linkers are required for MCM8/9 function.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes that the authors 'identified some important residues and motifs in MCM8-9 complex, mutations of which actually impaired the MCM8-9 activity in vitro and in vivo.' Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'a flexible nature of MCM8/9-CTD' as a strength. The combination of structural dynamics analysis and functional validation through both in vitro helicase assays and in vivo complementation experiments supports these claims.

results.result: Based on structural comparisons with MCM2-7 complexes (OCCM and DH), the authors propose that the gMCM8/9 structure represents a loading state of the helicase, as it is conformationally similar to the MCM2-7 loading intermediate OCCM rather than the double hexamer (DH).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states that 'they suggest that the observed gMCM8-9 structure might represent the structure of a loading state with possible DNA entry "gate"' and that overall 'the data presented would support the authors' conclusions.' However, this is an interpretive claim based on structural similarity rather than direct functional evidence. Reviewer 3's concern that 'the presented MCM8/9 structure is not a DNA-bound form' further limits the certainty of this functional assignment.

results.result: Structural analysis reveals that the trimer interface between MCM8/9 heterodimers is weaker than the dimer interface, being dominated by electrostatic and hydrogen-bonding interactions. The authors propose this weaker trimer interface could serve as a DNA entry 'gate,' as opening it would be easier than opening the dimer interface.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes that the authors 'suggest that the observed gMCM8-9 structure might represent the structure of a loading state with possible DNA entry "gate"' and that 'the data presented would support the authors' conclusions.' The structural characterization of interface interactions provides a reasonable basis for this proposal, though direct functional evidence of gate opening is not provided.

results.result: The authors identify conserved allosteric communication loop (ACL) residues in MCM8 through structural superposition with archaeal MCM. However, mutation of a key ACL residue (hMCM8_E295R) shows no significant effect on helicase activity, suggesting that MCM8's NTD does not interact with its CTD directly through ACL hairpins, unlike in archaeal MCMs.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 acknowledges that the authors 'identified some important residues and motifs in MCM8-9 complex, mutations of which actually impaired the MCM8-9 activity in vitro.' The negative result with the ACL mutant is supported by experimental data and leads to a mechanistic insight about differences between MCM8/9 and archaeal MCMs.

results.result: Cell viability assays show that MCM8- or MCM9-deficient DT40 cells are highly sensitive to cisplatin. Expression of wild-type MCM8 or MCM9 cDNAs almost completely rescues chemoresistance, while N-C linker deletion mutants have minimal complementary effects, demonstrating that N-C linkers are required for cellular resistance to DNA-damaging reagents.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states that the authors 'identified some important residues and motifs in MCM8-9 complex, mutations of which actually impaired the MCM8-9 activity in vitro and in vivo.' The in vivo functional validation through complementation assays provides strong support for the importance of the N-C linkers.

results.result: The authors acknowledge several limitations: the DNA substrate specificity of MCM8/9 is unknown, HROB only stimulates ~60% of MCM8/9 helicase activity suggesting other regulators exist, and high-resolution structures with DNA and nucleotides are needed to fully clarify the unwinding mechanism.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 emphasizes these limitations, stating 'additional studies are required to conclude this point because the presented MCM8/9 structure is not a DNA-bound form and HROB is not visible in the presented structural data.' Reviewer 3 specifically raised concerns about '(1) The presented structures exclusively depicted the unbound forms of DNA' and '(2) The MCM8/9 activator, HROB, was not visible in the structural data.' The authors' acknowledgment of these limitations aligns with reviewer concerns.

comparisons.comparison: Strong agreement on study limitations (C123-C127). Both acknowledge the absence of DNA-bound structures and incomplete HROB visualization. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED for honest acknowledgment of limitations, while peer reviewers emphasize these as critical gaps requiring additional studies.

Strong agreement on in vivo validation (C88-C91). Both recognize the cell viability assays and complementation experiments as strong support. OpenEval and peer reviewers (Reviewer 1) both rate these claims as SUPPORTED, noting that mutations impaired MCM8-9 activity in vivo.

Partial disagreement on structural claims (C2, C31-C36, C92). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on cryo-EM data quality. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 1 noting that 'most structural data are shown only as ribbon model without showing the density map data' and Reviewer 3 emphasizing the structure is 'not a DNA-bound form,' limiting mechanistic conclusions.

Agreement on ACL analysis (C69-C71, C75-C76). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the negative mutagenesis result is reasonable though could reflect redundancy. Peer reviewers (Reviewer 1) acknowledge the identification of important residues with functional validation.

Disagreement on HROB-induced conformational changes (C54-C63). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on combined structural and biochemical data. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 3 emphasizing that 'HROB was not visible in the structural data' and direct visualization of MCM8/9-HROB complex is essential.

Agreement on OB-hp functional importance (C64-C65, C67, C73-C74, C77, C103). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with caveat about DNA docking model. Peer reviewers (Reviewer 1) rate as SUPPORTED, noting identification of important residues with functional validation through helicase assays.

Agreement on N-C linker and CTD flexibility (C82, C84-C86, C120). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes reasonable inference connecting structural features to dynamics. Peer reviewers acknowledge flexible CTD nature and functional validation through mutational analysis in vitro and in vivo.

Agreement on CTD rotary motion (C5, C80-C81, C119). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes multi-body refinement supports flexibility but functional interpretation is inferred. Peer reviewers (Reviewer 3) acknowledge 'flexible nature of MCM8/9-CTD' as a strength with functional validation.

Agreement on DNA entry gate hypothesis (C42-C43, C46). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED noting the inference is reasonable but requires experimental validation. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, acknowledging the structural basis for the gate proposal though direct functional evidence is lacking.

Agreement on loading state interpretation (C51, C53). Both rate as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes this is a working hypothesis based on structural similarity. Peer reviewers note data support the conclusion but emphasize it's interpretive, with Reviewer 3 highlighting the structure is 'not a DNA-bound form.'

Agreement on helicase assay data (C72-C74). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on direct experimental evidence. Peer reviewers also support these claims as part of the biochemical validation that strengthens structural inferences.

Disagreement on HROB mechanism (C110, C113, C122). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with caveat that DNA loading mechanism is inferred. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, emphasizing the critical limitation that HROB is not visible in structural data, making mechanistic interpretation less certain.
